placed. However, there is no need to address this point. The lower court expressly assessed this 
finding as “not incorrect” (see E. 4.2.2 above) and did not view it per se as a violation of the non-
competition clause. This also applies when the defendant argues that he or Arkadium should have 
been permitted to inform the experts—or the individuals whose data was being processed—about 
the takeover of Construction21’s ongoing placement processes. This is undisputed. 
On the other hand, the defendant has still not presented any arguments that would demonstrate 
the lower court’s view—namely, that it was not necessary to mention the transfer of operational 
business in the letter when informing the experts (E. 4.2.3)—to be arbitrary. The defendant 
argues that, since the letter to the experts was addressed to all candidates in the database, the 
focus was on why Construction21’s data had ended up with Arkadium. This argument is not 
convincing. As the lower court correctly noted, it would have sufficed to state that, due to 
organizational changes, the experts would have to contact Arkadium as of October 1, 2020. 
Contrary to the defendant’s view, the lower court does not accuse him of failing to address, in his 
answer to the complaint or appeal, the alleged necessity of mentioning the transfer of operational 
business. Rather, it merely assessed the reasoning provided for this as implausible. This is 
understandable. 
Nor does the defendant’s argument against the lower court’s reasoning regarding the 
impermissibility of describing Arkadium as “a leading headhunter” hold water. The interpretation 
of the disputed passage as advertising—and thus as impermissible competition against the 
plaintiff—is convincing. This is not altered by the defendant’s assertion that Arkadium was 
required and permitted to indicate who it was, or that it, too, was a headhunter. The same applies 
to the argument that Arkadium had a legitimate interest in retaining the experts in its—
expensively acquired—database. Contrary to the defendant’s characterization, the reasoning of 
the lower court does not indicate that it considered the description as “one of the leading 
headhunters” to be unproblematic or permissible. Furthermore, it is irrelevant whether the 
recipients of the letter to the experts perceived it as competitive.  
Finally, the lower court addressed the defendant’s argument—that the disclosure of data was in 
the plaintiff’s interest and, in fact, its obligation—as part of its assessment of the amount of the 
contractual penalty (more on this below).
